title: First words
goal: Greet people the Pashtun way, say yes and no, thank someone and apologise politely.
intro:
Pashtuns greet generously: a simple hello is followed by a string of good wishes — Are you well? Are you happy? Is your family well? The everyday Islamic greeting **السلام عليکم** is used everywhere, and Pashto adds its own lovely greeting **ستړي مه شې** (stə́ṛi ma she, 'may you not be tired'), answered with **خوار مه شې** (xwār ma she, 'may you not be poor').

In this unit you'll learn these greetings, the polite words for thank you, please and sorry, and the two words for 'you'. Learn the phrases as whole chunks and say them aloud.

vocab.note: Used by everyone, at any time of day. Often shortened to سلام salā́m.

vocab.en: hello (lit. may you not be tired)
vocab.note: Typical Pashto greeting, especially to someone arriving or working. To a group: ستړي مه شئ stə́ṛi ma shəy.

vocab.en: reply to ستړي مه شې (lit. may you not be poor)

vocab.note: To a group or politely: په خير راغلئ pə xayr rā́ġləy.

vocab.en: welcome (formal, on signs and in speeches)

vocab.note: Placed before the verb to negate: نه يم na yəm 'I am not'.
Agrees with feminine nouns: ډېره مننه ḍéra manə́na 'thank you very much'.
f. مهرباني وکړئ 'please (do the kindness)'; also said alone as 'thanks'.
f. بښنه غواړم 'I'm sorry'. Also spelt بخښنه.
m. خير دی 'it's fine, never mind'; په خير 'safely'.

vocab.en: have a good journey (said to someone leaving)

vocab.note: As 'OK!' alone: ښه. Feminine ښه ṣa.

vocab.en: well, in good health (lit. made, built)
vocab.note: جوړ يې؟ 'Are you well?' — part of every greeting. f. جوړه.
For friends, children, equals and God.
Use with elders, strangers, officials. Southern dialects: تاسې tā́se.

vocab.en: how wonderful (lit. what God has willed)
vocab.note: Said when admiring a child, a house, success — instead of plain praise.

vocab.en: sir, Mr (after a name or title)

vocab.note: احمد جان ahmád jān. Affectionate and very common.
پوه شوم 'I understood', پوه نه شوم 'I didn't understand'.

phrases.note: Afghans often say تاسو څنګه ياست؟ tāso tsə́nga yāst?

phrases.en: Are you well? Are you good?
phrases.note: Said together as one friendly greeting.

phrases.en: Fine, thank God. And how are you?
See you again. (lit. we'll see each other again)
Thank you for your hospitality! (lit. may your house flourish)

grammar.title: Word order: the verb comes last
grammar.body:
Pashto is a **subject–object–verb (SOV)** language. Where English says 'I drink tea', Pashto says 'I tea drink': زه چای څښم. Even 'X is Y' sentences put the verb 'to be' at the end: 'I fine am' — زه ښه يم.

The negative نه (na) goes directly before the verb: زه ستړی **نه** يم 'I am not tired'.

The present tense of 'to be' is worth memorising now:
زه يم zə yəm — I am
ته يې tə ye — you are (informal)
هغه دی haġá day — he is / هغه ده haġá da — she is
موږ يو muẓ yu — we are
تاسو يئ tāso yəy — you are (polite/plural)
هغوی دي haġwí di — they are

examples.en: I am fine. (lit. I good am)
I drink tea. (lit. I tea drink)
He speaks Pashto. (lit. he Pashto says)

grammar.title: Two kinds of 'you': ته and تاسو
grammar.body:
Pashto has an informal **ته** (tə) for one close friend, a child or a younger relative, and a polite **تاسو** (tāso) for elders, strangers and anyone you want to honour — تاسو is also the plural 'you (all)'. When in doubt, use تاسو.

The verb changes too: with ته the verb ends in **-e** (spelt ې), with تاسو it ends in **-əy** (spelt ئ). So 'are you well?' is ته جوړ يې؟ (tə joṛ ye?) to a friend, but تاسو جوړ يئ؟ (tāso joṛ yəy?) to an elder. Imperatives work the same way: مهرباني وکړه (informal) vs مهرباني وکړئ (polite).

examples.en: Are you tired? (informal, to a man)

dialogue.title: Meeting an elder in the village
dialogue.setting: Ahmad, a young man, comes home to his village and meets Haji Gul Khan, an elderly neighbour, in the lane.

lines.speaker: Haji Gul Khan
lines.native: وعليکم السلام، احمد جان! په خير راغلې.
lines.roman: wa ʿaláykum assalā́m, ahmád jān! pə xayr rā́ġle.

lines.speaker: Ahmad
lines.native: مننه. تاسو څنګه يئ؟ جوړ يئ؟
lines.roman: manə́na. tāso tsə́nga yəy? joṛ yəy?
lines.en: Thank you. How are you? Are you well?

lines.speaker: Haji Gul Khan
lines.native: شکر، ښه يم. ته جوړ يې؟ ستړی خو نه يې؟
lines.roman: shukr, ṣə yəm. tə joṛ ye? stə́ṛay xo na ye?
lines.en: Fine, thank God. Are you well? You're not tired, are you?

lines.speaker: Ahmad
lines.native: نه، ستړی نه يم. ډېره مننه.
lines.roman: na, stə́ṛay na yəm. ḍéra manə́na.
lines.en: No, I'm not tired. Thank you very much.

lines.speaker: Ahmad
lines.native: بښنه غواړم، حاجي صاحب، اوس کور ته ځم. انشاالله بيا.
lines.roman: baṣə́na ġwā́ṛəm, hājí sāhíb, os kor ta dzəm. inshāllā́h biyā́.
lines.en: Sorry, Haji sahib, I'm going home now. Another time, God willing.

lines.speaker: Haji Gul Khan
lines.native: سمه ده. کور ته مې سلام ووايه.
lines.roman: sáma da. kor ta me salā́m wə́wāya.
lines.en: All right. Give my greetings to your family (lit. house).

culture: Greetings among Pashtuns are long and warm: after السلام عليکم come questions like جوړ يې؟ ښه يې؟ خوشاله يې؟ کور کلی دې ښه دی؟ ('Are you well? good? happy? Are your home and village well?'), and both people may ask at the same time — you don't have to answer each one. The younger person or the one arriving greets first, and elders are addressed with تاسو and titles like حاجي صاحب, ماما (uncle) or ادې (mother). Men shake hands, often with both hands, and friends embrace; between unrelated men and women a respectful greeting is usually given without physical contact — a nod with the right hand on the heart is always appropriate. If you're thanked for something, answer هېڅ خبره نه ده or simply شکر.
